ch36.note: A temple to the Medicine King (药王, the deified master of healing). The Hebei town of Anguo, built around its great Medicine King temple, was for centuries China's foremost market for medicinal herbs—which is why an army report places a fugitive there.

Under the emperors, red ink was the sovereign's alone: his terse annotations on a memorial, written in the 'vermilion brush,' were the imperial rescript. To sign off in red thus carried an air of final, absolute authority.
Liu Bocheng (刘伯承, 1892–1986), the one-eyed Communist general known as a master tactician, commander of what became the Second Field Army and later one of the ten marshals of the People's Republic.

'Settling accounts' (清算): the organized mass meetings of Communist land reform at which peasants were marshaled to confront landlords and former officials, tally their alleged wrongs, and strip them of land and goods—often violently.
The Jin-Cha-Ji Border Region (晋察冀), spanning Shanxi (Jin), Chahar (Cha), and Hebei (Ji)—the first great Communist base established behind Japanese lines, built up under Nie Rongzhen.

Hu Zongnan (胡宗南, 1896–1962), a leading Nationalist general and Chiang loyalist commanding the northwest front, who stormed and took the Communist capital of Yan'an in March 1947—a hollow triumph, as the Communists had already withdrawn.

Fu Dongju (傅冬菊, 1924–2007), daughter of the Nationalist commander Fu Zuoyi and a secret member of the Communist Party, who acted as a go-between and helped bring about her father's peaceful surrender of Beiping in January 1949.

ch36.anchor: washing of the brain and the changing of the heart
ch36.note: A near-literal rendering of the Chinese xinao (洗脑), 'to wash the brain.' It is the very term from which the English word 'brainwashing' was coined, around 1950, to describe the Chinese Communists' methods of forced ideological remolding.

'Speak-bitterness' meetings (诉苦, suku): a standard Communist mobilization technique in which people were led to recount their past sufferings in public and so be roused to denounce landlords, officials, and other class enemies.
